claim: Pancreatic α-cells secrete glucagon, an insulin counter-regulatory peptide hormone critical for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
source: Pancreatic α-cells secrete glucagon, an insulin counter-regulatory peptide hormone critical for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about α-cell function.

claim: Investigation of the function of human α-cells remains a challenge due to the lack of cost-effective purification methods to isolate high-quality α-cells from islets.
source: Investigation of the function of human α-cells remains a challenge due to the lack of cost-effective purification methods to isolate high-quality α-cells from islets.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field, supported by the context of the study.

claim: DA-ZP1 can be used to enrich live α-cells from dissociated human islet cells with ~95% purity.
source: Here, we use the reaction-based probe diacetylated Zinpyr1 (DA-ZP1) to introduce a novel and simple method for enriching live α-cells from dissociated human islet cells with ~95% purity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing immunostaining results and quantification in Figure 1.

claim: The α-cells sorted by DA-ZP1 were confirmed by sorting and immunostaining for glucagon.
source: The α-cells, confirmed by sorting and immunostaining for glucagon, were cultured up to 10 days to form α-pseudoislets.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Sorted α-cells can be cultured up to 10 days to form α-pseudoislets.
source: The α-cells, confirmed by sorting and immunostaining for glucagon, were cultured up to 10 days to form α-pseudoislets.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing culture and morphology in Figure 2.

claim: α-pseudoislets can be maintained in culture without significant loss of viability.
source: The α-pseudoislets could be maintained in culture without significant loss of viability, and responded to glucose challenge by secreting appropriate levels of glucagon.
evidence: Supported by ATP-based viability assay data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: α-pseudoislets respond to glucose challenge by secreting appropriate levels of glucagon.
source: The α-pseudoislets could be maintained in culture without significant loss of viability, and responded to glucose challenge by secreting appropriate levels of glucagon.
evidence: Supported by glucagon secretion assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Expression levels of key α-cell identity genes were sustained in culture in α-pseudoislets.
source: RNA-sequencing analyses (RNA-seq) revealed that expression levels of key α-cell identity genes were sustained in culture while some of the genes such as DLK1, GSN, SMIM24 were altered in α-pseudoislets in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DLK1, GSN, and SMIM24 gene expression were altered in α-pseudoislets in a time-dependent manner.
source: RNA-sequencing analyses (RNA-seq) revealed that expression levels of key α-cell identity genes were sustained in culture while some of the genes such as DLK1, GSN, SMIM24 were altered in α-pseudoislets in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunostaining data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Newport Green (NPG) has been employed previously for the purification of human or murine α-cells and β-cells.
source: Zinc-binding molecules such as Newport Green (NPG) (Kirkpatrick et al., 2010) and ZIGIR (zinc granule indicator) (Ghazvini Zadeh et al., 2020) have been employed previously for the purification of human or murine α-cells and β-cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ZIGIR has been employed previously for the purification of human or murine α-cells and β-cells.
source: Zinc-binding molecules such as Newport Green (NPG) (Kirkpatrick et al., 2010) and ZIGIR (zinc granule indicator) (Ghazvini Zadeh et al., 2020) have been employed previously for the purification of human or murine α-cells and β-cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPG was reported to sort cell population with 75% enriched α-cells.
source: While NPG was reported to sort cell population with 75% enriched α-cells, ZIGIR enabled isolation of >95% pure α-cells when used in combination with antibodies specific to endocrine cells and α-cells such as HPi2 (Dorrell et al., 2008) and TM4S4F (Muraro et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and comparison with current method.

claim: ZIGIR enabled isolation of >95% pure α-cells when used in combination with antibodies specific to endocrine cells and α-cells such as HPi2 and TM4S4F.
source: While NPG was reported to sort cell population with 75% enriched α-cells, ZIGIR enabled isolation of >95% pure α-cells when used in combination with antibodies specific to endocrine cells and α-cells such as HPi2 (Dorrell et al., 2008) and TM4S4F (Muraro et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DA-ZP1 has been used to purify human pancreatic β-cells.
source: We have recently reported the purification of human pancreatic β-cells (Lee et al., 2020) and stem-cell derived β-like cells (Kahraman et al., 2021) using the zinc-based reaction probe diacetylated Zinpyr1 (DA-ZP1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: DA-ZP1 has been used to purify stem-cell derived β-like cells.
source: We have recently reported the purification of human pancreatic β-cells (Lee et al., 2020) and stem-cell derived β-like cells (Kahraman et al., 2021) using the zinc-based reaction probe diacetylated Zinpyr1 (DA-ZP1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: DA-ZP1 is a non-fluorescent zinc sensor that binds Zn(II) with nanomolar affinity.
source: DA-ZP1 is a non-fluorescent zinc sensor that binds Zn(II) with nanomolar affinity (Chyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization study.

claim: Binding of Zn(II) to DA-ZP1 selectively and rapidly mediates hydrolytic cleavage of the acetyl groups and generates a strong fluorescence.
source: Binding of Zn(II) selectively and rapidly mediates hydrolytic cleavage of the acetyl groups and generates a strong fluorescence to sort the labeled cells by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of DA-ZP1, supported by citation and established knowledge.

claim: FACS analysis of DA-ZP1-stained human islet cells showed enrichment of β-cells in the DA-ZP1 positive population.
source: In Lee et al., we performed FACS analysis of DA-ZP1-stained human islets cells and observed enrichment of β-cells in the DA-ZP1 positive population (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DA-ZP1 positive cells can be reclassified as either 'DA-ZP1 intermediate' or 'DA-ZP1 bright' by distinctly marking the boundary among the fractions.
source: We reclassified DA-ZP1 positive cells as either 'DA-ZP1 intermediate' or 'DA-ZP1 bright' by distinctly marking the boundary among the fractions to contrast those with 'bright' DA-ZP1 fluorescence that were identified as β-cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: High purity α-cells and β-cells can be generated by simultaneously sorting islet cells using DA-ZP1.
source: These data indicate that high purity α-cells and β-cells can be generated by simultaneously sorting islet cells using a zinc reaction probe (DA-ZP1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing purity of sorted populations in Figure 1.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of DA-ZP1-labeled dispersed human islet cells showed a wide spread of fluorescence intensity on a two-dimensional density plot.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of the cells showed a wide spread of fluorescence intensity among dispersed islet cells on a two-dimensional density plot.
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: DA-ZP1-labeled islet cells can be classified into three subsets based on their fluorescence intensity: 'low', 'intermediate', and 'bright'.
source: We classified the cells into three subsets based on their fluorescence intensity and drew a gate to separate each of the subsets (Figure 1b). The subset centered near the unstained cell background showed 'low' fluorescence intensity while the other two cell populations positioned on the right side of the dot-plot showed 'intermediate' and 'bright' fluorescence intensities, respectively (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DA-ZP1 labeling resulted in a similar fluorescence intensity pattern among the three cell populations (low, intermediate, bright) in four independent human islet donors.
source: We confirmed that DA-ZP1 labeling resulted in a similar fluorescence intensity pattern among the three cell populations (low, intermediate, bright) in an additional four independent human islet donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FACS data from multiple donors shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DA-ZP1 'bright' subset displayed higher fluorescence signal compared to the intermediate subset as validated by fluorescent microscopy.
source: Consistent with the FACS-based fluorescence assessment, fluorescent microscopy validated that the DA-ZP1 'bright' subset displayed higher fluorescence signal compared to the intermediate subset, and that the unsorted islet cells are comprised of a mixture of cells with varying fluorescence intensities (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Unsorted islet cells are comprised of a mixture of cells with varying fluorescence intensities.
source: Consistent with the FACS-based fluorescence assessment, fluorescent microscopy validated that the DA-ZP1 'bright' subset displayed higher fluorescence signal compared to the intermediate subset, and that the unsorted islet cells are comprised of a mixture of cells with varying fluorescence intensities (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The bright subset was highly enriched for human β-cells (~83% CPEP+ cells).
source: Immunofluorescence analysis showed that the bright subset was highly enriched for human β-cells (~83% CPEP+ cells), while the intermediate subset consisted of α-cells of high purity (~95% GCG+ cells) (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The intermediate subset consisted of α-cells of high purity (~95% GCG+ cells).
source: Immunofluorescence analysis showed that the bright subset was highly enriched for human β-cells (~83% CPEP+ cells), while the intermediate subset consisted of α-cells of high purity (~95% GCG+ cells) (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The cells in the DA-ZP1 'low' subset were mostly hormone negative.
source: The cells in the DA-ZP1 'low' subset were mostly hormone negative, indicating that these cells likely represented non-hormonal cells such as fibroblast-like, endothelial, or exocrine cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The DA-ZP1 'low' subset likely represented non-hormonal cells such as fibroblast-like, endothelial, or exocrine cells.
source: The cells in the DA-ZP1 'low' subset were mostly hormone negative, indicating that these cells likely represented non-hormonal cells such as fibroblast-like, endothelial, or exocrine cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hormone-negative status of these cells.

claim: Expression levels of α-cell markers such as GCG, TTR, ARX, IRX1, IRX2 are higher in the intermediate subset compared to other subsets.
source: Consistently, transcriptomics analysis of three different populations by RNA-seq showed that the expression levels of α-cell markers such as GCG, TTR, ARX, IRX1, IRX2 are higher in the intermediate subset, the expression levels of β-cell markers such as INS, MAFA, PDX1, IAPP are higher in the bright subset, and the expression levels of non-endocrine cell markers such as CFTR, KRT19, VIM are higher in the low subset compared to other subsets (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Expression levels of β-cell markers such as INS, MAFA, PDX1, IAPP are higher in the bright subset compared to other subsets.
source: Consistently, transcriptomics analysis of three different populations by RNA-seq showed that the expression levels of α-cell markers such as GCG, TTR, ARX, IRX1, IRX2 are higher in the intermediate subset, the expression levels of β-cell markers such as INS, MAFA, PDX1, IAPP are higher in the bright subset, and the expression levels of non-endocrine cell markers such as CFTR, KRT19, VIM are higher in the low subset compared to other subsets (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Expression levels of non-endocrine cell markers such as CFTR, KRT19, VIM are higher in the low subset compared to other subsets.
source: Consistently, transcriptomics analysis of three different populations by RNA-seq showed that the expression levels of α-cell markers such as GCG, TTR, ARX, IRX1, IRX2 are higher in the intermediate subset, the expression levels of β-cell markers such as INS, MAFA, PDX1, IAPP are higher in the bright subset, and the expression levels of non-endocrine cell markers such as CFTR, KRT19, VIM are higher in the low subset compared to other subsets (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The low expression levels of SST, HHEX, GHRL, and PPY in the intermediate subset compared to other subsets indicate a small amount of contamination with other endocrine islet cell types such as delta, epsilon, and PP cells.
source: The low expression levels of SST, HHEX, GHRL, and PPY in the intermediate subset compared to other subsets indicate a small amount of contamination with the other endocrine islet cell types such as delta, epsilon, and PP cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: DA-ZP1-stained cells and NPG-stained cells formed a single bright cluster with no distinct intermediate population to separate α-cells from β-cells easily.
source: While DA-ZP1 generated three distinct clusters of cells with low, intermediate, or bright fluorescence, ZIGIR-stained cells and NPG-stained cells formed a single bright cluster with no distinct intermediate population to separate α-cells from β-cells easily (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by FACS comparison data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: DA-ZP1 generated three distinct clusters of cells with low, intermediate, or bright fluorescence.
source: While DA-ZP1 generated three distinct clusters of cells with low, intermediate, or bright fluorescence, ZIGIR-stained cells and NPG-stained cells formed a single bright cluster with no distinct intermediate population to separate α-cells from β-cells easily (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by FACS comparison data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: DA-ZP1 is unique in its ability to label α-cells without the aid of an antibody-based approach making it superior to other zinc-based molecules.
source: These data show that DA-ZP1 is unique in its ability to label α-cells without the aid of an antibody-based approach making it superior to other zinc-based molecules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Both sorted α-cells and unsorted islet cells formed islet-like clusters shortly after seeding in round-bottom non-treated plates.
source: Both the sorted α-cells and the unsorted islet cells formed islet-like clusters shortly after seeding in round-bottom non-treated plates (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by bright-field microscopy images shown in Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: α-pseudoislets tended to form tighter clusters shortly after plating compared to unsorted pseudoislets.
source: Interestingly, α-pseudoislets tended to form tighter clusters shortly after plating compared to unsorted pseudoislets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Culturing cells for up to 10 days did not alter viability of α-pseudoislets and unsorted pseudoislets.
source: Culturing cells for up to 10 days did not alter viability of α-pseudoislets and unsorted pseudoislets indicating that these cells can be maintained in culture without significant cell loss.
evidence: Supported by ATP-based viability assay data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Native islets started to die after day 5 possibly due to necrosis in the core of the islets caused by hypoxia.
source: In contrast, native islets started to die after day 5 possibly due to necrosis in the core of the islets caused by hypoxia (Giuliani et al., 2005; Komatsu et al., 2017; Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by viability data in Figure 2d and citations to previous studies on islet hypoxia.

claim: α-pseudoislets consisted of a highly pure population of α-cells with ~95% GCG+ cells on days 5 and 10.
source: We further validated that α-pseudoislets consisted of a highly pure population of α-cells with ~95% GCG+ cells on days 5 and 10 (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e and 2f.

claim: Apoptosis index remained stable over the duration of the culture in both α-pseudoislets and in unsorted pseudoislets.
source: Apoptosis index remained stable over the duration of the culture in both α-pseudoislets and in unsorted pseudoislets indicating that α-cells survived even after they form pseudoislets (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2g and 2h.

claim: The percentage of apoptotic α-cells in native islets tend to increase on day 10 compared to day 5 which could be due to hypoxia.
source: However, the percentage of apoptotic α-cells in native islets tend to increase on day 10 compared to day 5 which could be due to hypoxia (Komatsu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 2h and citation to previous work on islet hypoxia.

claim: Proliferating α-cells were observed in α-pseudoislets, unsorted pseudoislets, and native islets on both days 5 and 10.
source: Notably, we observed proliferating α-cells in α-pseudoislets, unsorted pseudoislets, and native islets on both days 5 and 10 (Figure 2i).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Percentage of Ki67+GCG+ cells was similar in each group on day 5 (α-pseudoislets; 0.038%±0.008, unsorted pseudoislets; 0.049%±0.007, native islets; 0.031%±0.004).
source: Percentage of Ki67+GCG+ cells was similar in each group on day 5 (α-pseudoislets; 0.038%±0.008, unsorted pseudoislets; 0.049%±0.007, native islets; 0.031%±0.004) and did not alter significantly with time spent in culture indicating that α-cells maintained their proliferation potential in culture (Figure 2j).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 quantification data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Percentage of Ki67+GCG+ cells did not alter significantly with time spent in culture indicating that α-cells maintained their proliferation potential in culture.
source: Percentage of Ki67+GCG+ cells was similar in each group on day 5 (α-pseudoislets; 0.038%±0.008, unsorted pseudoislets; 0.049%±0.007, native islets; 0.031%±0.004) and did not alter significantly with time spent in culture indicating that α-cells maintained their proliferation potential in culture (Figure 2j).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 quantification data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Glucagon release significantly decreased in response to high glucose treatment in α-pseudoislets, unsorted pseudoislets, and native islets.
source: Glucagon release significantly decreased in response to high glucose treatment in each group (Figure 3b), while the fold increase between low (3.3 mM) or high (16.7 mM) glucose were comparable among the groups (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by glucagon secretion assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The fold increase in glucagon secretion between low (3.3 mM) or high (16.7 mM) glucose were comparable among α-pseudoislets, unsorted pseudoislets, and native islets.
source: Glucagon release significantly decreased in response to high glucose treatment in each group (Figure 3b), while the fold increase between low (3.3 mM) or high (16.7 mM) glucose were comparable among the groups (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by glucagon secretion assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Unsorted pseudoislets displayed higher basal secretion of glucagon compared to native islets which is consistent with previous observation.
source: Unsorted pseudoislets displayed higher basal secretion of glucagon compared to native islets which is consistent with the previous observation (Reissaus and Piston, 2017).
evidence: Supported by glucagon secretion data in Figure 3b and citation to previous work.

claim: α-Pseudoislets showed higher glucagon content compared to unsorted pseudoislets.
source: α-Pseudoislets showed higher glucagon content compared to unsorted pseudoislets (Figure 3d), indicating high purity of sorted glucagon positive cells.
evidence: Supported by glucagon content measurement data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Higher glucagon content in α-pseudoislets indicates high purity of sorted glucagon positive cells.
source: α-Pseudoislets showed higher glucagon content compared to unsorted pseudoislets (Figure 3d), indicating high purity of sorted glucagon positive cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on glucagon content data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: α-pseudoislets are similar to unsorted pseudoislets in their capacity for glucose-responsive glucagon secretion.
source: These results indicate that α-pseudoislets are similar to unsorted pseudoislets in their capacity for glucose-responsive glucagon secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on glucagon secretion data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Analysis of scRNA-seq data from cadaveric human islets revealed 75 α-cell enriched genes and 68 β-cell enriched genes.
source: Analysis of scRNA-seq data revealed 75 α-cell enriched genes and 68 β-cell enriched genes in cadaveric islet α-cells and β-cells, respectively (false discovery rate [FDR]<0.1, fold change [FC]>1.5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available scRNA-seq data (GSE84133) from Baron et al., 2016.

claim: 20 (27%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes including GCG, TTR, IRX2 were upregulated in α-pseudoislets compared to unsorted pseudoislets or native islets on day 0.
source: Expression analysis of α-cell enriched and β-cell enriched genes in α-pseudoislets showed that 20 (27%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes including GCG, TTR, IRX2 were upregulated and 24 (35%) of the 68 β-cell enriched genes including INS, IAPP, MAFA, PDX1, NKX6-1, G6PC2 were downregulated in α-pseudoislets compared to unsorted pseudoislets or native islets on day 0 (FDR < 0.1; FC > 2 or FC < –2, Supplementary file 2), which confirms the enrichment of α-cells in α-pseudoislets (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 24 (35%) of the 68 β-cell enriched genes including INS, IAPP, MAFA, PDX1, NKX6-1, G6PC2 were downregulated in α-pseudoislets compared to unsorted pseudoislets or native islets on day 0.
source: Expression analysis of α-cell enriched and β-cell enriched genes in α-pseudoislets showed that 20 (27%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes including GCG, TTR, IRX2 were upregulated and 24 (35%) of the 68 β-cell enriched genes including INS, IAPP, MAFA, PDX1, NKX6-1, G6PC2 were downregulated in α-pseudoislets compared to unsorted pseudoislets or native islets on day 0 (FDR < 0.1; FC > 2 or FC < –2, Supplementary file 2), which confirms the enrichment of α-cells in α-pseudoislets (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 61 (~81%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes did not alter in α-pseudoislets on day 5 and day 10 compared to day 0.
source: Concurrently, 61 (~81%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes did not alter in α-pseudoislets on day 5 and day 10 compared to day 0 (FDR < 0.1; FC < –2 and FC > 2, Supplementary file 3, Figure 4b), indicating the majority of the α-cell enriched genes including GCG, ARX, IRX2, and TTR were preserved in culture.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The majority of the α-cell enriched genes including GCG, ARX, IRX2, and TTR were preserved in culture in α-pseudoislets.
source: Concurrently, 61 (~81%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes did not alter in α-pseudoislets on day 5 and day 10 compared to day 0 (FDR < 0.1; FC < –2 and FC > 2, Supplementary file 3, Figure 4b), indicating the majority of the α-cell enriched genes including GCG, ARX, IRX2, and TTR were preserved in culture.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: 53 (71%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes and 49 (72%) of the 68 β-cell enriched genes did not alter in unsorted pseudoislets on day 5 compared to day 0.
source: Similarly, 53 (71%) of the 75 α-cell enriched genes and 49 (72%) of the 68 β-cell enriched genes did not alter in unsorted pseudoislets on day 5 compared to day 0.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Genes differentially expressed in unsorted pseudoislets on day 5 compared to day 0 were unchanged on day 10 compared to day 0.
source: However, these genes differentially expressed in unsorted pseudoislets on day 5 compared to day 0 were unchanged on day 10 compared to day 0.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Existence of other islet cells and paracrine interactions in the unsorted pseudoislets were important for maintenance of α-cell or β-cell identity.
source: This might indicate that existence of other islet cells and paracrine interactions in the unsorted pseudoislets were important for maintenance of α-cell or β-cell identity (Cigliola et al., 2018; Figure 4b, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Native islets did not show any changes in expression levels of α-cell enriched or β-cell enriched genes on days 5 and 10 compared to day 0.
source: On the other hand, native islets did not show any changes in expression levels of α-cell enriched or β-cell enriched genes on days 5 and 10 compared to day 0 indicated that maintenance of islet structure was likely necessary to maintain cell identity.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Maintenance of islet structure was likely necessary to maintain cell identity.
source: On the other hand, native islets did not show any changes in expression levels of α-cell enriched or β-cell enriched genes on days 5 and 10 compared to day 0 indicated that maintenance of islet structure was likely necessary to maintain cell identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Co-existence of other cells and intact islet architecture were desirable but not indispensable for maintenance of α-cell identity in vitro.
source: In sum, comparison of α-pseudoislets, unsorted pseudoislets, and native islets on days 0, 5, 10 showed that co-existence of other cells and intact islet architecture were desirable but not indispensable for maintenance of α-cell identity in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Differential expression analysis yielded 4, 299, and 137 DEGs between unsorted pseudoislets and native islets on days 0, 5, and 10, respectively.
source: Differential expression analysis yielded 4, 299, and 137 DEGs on days 0, 5, and 10, respectively (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The gene expression profile of unsorted pseudoislets was almost identical to native islets on day 0.
source: Not surprisingly, the gene expression profile of unsorted pseudoislets was almost identical to native islets on day 0 (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: CCN2, DUSP5, NR4A1, and NR4A2 were significantly upregulated in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets on day 0.
source: For example, we detected differences in expression levels between the groups for only four genes, namely, CCN2 (cellular communication network factor 2), DUSP5 (dual specificity phosphatase 5), NR4A1 (nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 1), NR4A2 (nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 2) on day 0 (Figure 4d). All four genes were significantly upregulated in unsorted pseudoislets which indicates that dissociation of native islets into single cells triggered acute changes in their expression.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Dissociation of native islets into single cells triggered acute changes in expression of CCN2, DUSP5, NR4A1, and NR4A2.
source: All four genes were significantly upregulated in unsorted pseudoislets which indicates that dissociation of native islets into single cells triggered acute changes in their expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: 297 genes were downregulated and 2 (GHRL, AC10875.5) were upregulated in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets on day 5.
source: We detected changes in expression levels of 299 genes on day 5, among which 297 were downregulated and 2 (GHRL, AC10875.5) were upregulated in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: All 137 genes that were altered significantly in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets on day 10 were downregulated.
source: On day 10, all the 137 genes that were altered significantly in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets were downregulated (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: 127 genes were consistently downregulated on day 5 as well as day 10 in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets.
source: Among these, 127 genes were consistently downregulated on day 5 as well as day 10.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: Pathway analysis of commonly downregulated genes on days 5 and 10 in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets showed changes in pathways such as extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, integrin cell surface interactions, degradation of the ECM, complement system, and focal adhesion.
source: Pathway analysis of commonly downregulated genes on days 5 and 10 in the unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets showed changes in pathways such as extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, integrin cell surface interactions, degradation of the ECM, complement system, and focal adhesion supporting the notion that the differences were likely due to physical separation of islets into single cells (Figure 4g, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The differences in gene expression between unsorted pseudoislets and native islets were likely due to physical separation of islets into single cells.
source: Pathway analysis of commonly downregulated genes on days 5 and 10 in the unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets showed changes in pathways such as extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, integrin cell surface interactions, degradation of the ECM, complement system, and focal adhesion supporting the notion that the differences were likely due to physical separation of islets into single cells (Figure 4g, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Genes involved in the Hippo signaling pathway such as TEAD2, YAP1, WWTR1, TGFB2, CCN2 were consistently downregulated on days 5 and 10 in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets.
source: Interestingly, we observed consistent downregulation of genes involved in the Hippo signaling pathway such as TEAD2, YAP1, WWTR1, TGFB2, CCN2 on days 5 and 10.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Expression of CCN2 showed a dynamic change with upregulation on day 0 and downregulation on days 5 and 10 in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets.
source: Expression of CCN2 showed a dynamic change with upregulation on day 0 and downregulation on days 5 and 10 in unsorted pseudoislets compared to native islets.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 413 genes in α-pseudoislets, and 341 genes in unsorted pseudoislets, in contrast to only 11 genes in native islets were significantly altered during the period from day 0 to day 5 and day 5 to day 10.
source: We identified 413 genes in α-pseudoislets, and 341 genes in unsorted pseudoislets, in contrast to only 11 genes in native islets that were significantly altered during this period (Figure 5a, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A majority of the genes (597 out of 608 genes) that were altered during the culture period in α-pseudoislets and unsorted pseudoislets but not in native islets likely reflects a transcriptional response of the cells following cell dissociation and re-aggregation.
source: The fact that a majority of the genes (597 out of 608 genes) that were altered during this period in α-pseudoislets and unsorted pseudoislets but not in native islets likely reflects a transcriptional response of the cells following cell dissociation and re-aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Pathway analyses of 597 genes that were altered in α-pseudoislets or in unsorted pseudoislets but not in native islets revealed networks such as ECM organization, integrin cell surface interaction, focal adhesion, and collagen formation.
source: Pathway analyses of these 597 genes that were altered in α-pseudoislets or in unsorted pseudoislets but not in native islets revealed networks such as ECM organization, integrin cell surface interaction, focal adhesion, and collagen formation (Figure 5b, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Among the 263 genes altered over the period of culture exclusively in α-pseudoislets, 110 genes were upregulated and 153 genes were downregulated.
source: Among the 263 genes, 110 genes were upregulated and 153 genes were downregulated.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Genes including MT1E, MT1X, and MT2A belonging to the metallothionein gene family and pathways such as response to metal ions, metallothioneins bind metals, and mineral absorption were upregulated in α-pseudoislets.
source: We observed that genes including MT1E (metallothionein 1E), MT1X (metallothionein 1X), and MT2A (metallothionein 2A) belonging to the metallothionein gene family and the pathways such as response to metal ions, metallothioneins bind metals, and mineral absorption were upregulated in α-pseudoislets (Figure 5c and d, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and pathway analysis data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: Previous studies have identified variant alleles of metallothionein genes and their association with type 2 diabetes.
source: Previous studies have identified variant alleles of metallothionein genes and their association with type 2 diabetes (Yang et al., 2008); however, their role in α-cells is not fully explored.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The role of metallothionein genes in α-cells is not fully explored.
source: Previous studies have identified variant alleles of metallothionein genes and their association with type 2 diabetes (Yang et al., 2008); however, their role in α-cells is not fully explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Pathways such as FoxO signaling, apoptosis, cell-ECM interactions, cGMP-PKG signaling, MAPK signaling, insulin secretion, and glucagon signaling pathway were all downregulated in the α-pseudoislets.
source: Interestingly, pathways such as FoxO signaling, apoptosis, cell-ECM interactions, cGMP-PKG signaling, MAPK signaling, insulin secretion, and glucagon signaling pathway were all downregulated in the α-pseudoislets (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: The β-cell enriched genes, DLK1 and GSN were downregulated significantly over time in α-pseudoislets.
source: We observed that the β-cell enriched genes, DLK1 (delta like non-canonical Notch ligand 1) also known as Pref-1, and GSN (gelsolin) were also downregulated significantly over time in α-pseudoislets (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: SMIM24, one of the α-cell enriched genes, was upregulated significantly in α-pseudoislets with time.
source: On the other hand, SMIM24 (small integral membrane protein 24), one of the α-cell enriched genes, was upregulated significantly in α-pseudoislets with time (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: α-cells express SMIM24, GSN, and DLK1 and expression of these proteins altered with time.
source: Using immunostaining, we validated that α-cells express SMIM24, GSN, and DLK1 and expression of these proteins altered with time (Figure 5e and f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5e and 5f.

claim: Human pancreatic α-cells can be purified by cell dissociation followed by DA-ZP1 labeling and FACS.
source: Overall, this study shows that human pancreatic α-cells can be purified by cell dissociation followed by DA-ZP1 labeling and FACS, and the purified α-cells can be maintained in culture to study secretory function, transcriptional changes, survival, and proliferation of α-cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented.

claim: Purified α-cells can be maintained in culture to study secretory function, transcriptional changes, survival, and proliferation of α-cells.
source: Overall, this study shows that human pancreatic α-cells can be purified by cell dissociation followed by DA-ZP1 labeling and FACS, and the purified α-cells can be maintained in culture to study secretory function, transcriptional changes, survival, and proliferation of α-cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented.

claim: The progress in studies related to human α-cell biology has been relatively slower compared to β-cells.
source: Despite its importance in both physiology and pathophysiology, the progress in studies related to human α-cell biology has been relatively slower compared to β-cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: A major limitation in α-cell research is the technical challenge in obtaining adequate numbers of high-quality live human α-cells for analyses.
source: A major limitation is the technical challenge in obtaining adequate numbers of high-quality live human α-cells for analyses (Haliyur et al., 2019; Xin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Live human α-cells were purified from human islet preparations by using a panel of cell-surface-binding monoclonal antibodies in previous studies.
source: In previous studies, live human α-cells were purified from human islet preparations by using a panel of cell-surface-binding monoclonal antibodies (Dorrell et al., 2008) or by combining antibody labeling approaches with ZIGIR labeling (Ghazvini Zadeh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both antibody-based and ZIGIR-based methods enable isolation of live human α-cells with high purity, but require antibody staining.
source: Both methods enable isolation of live human α-cells with high purity, but require antibody staining, which increases the risk of cell loss during the labeling procedure and consequently limits α-cell yield.
evidence: This is a statement about previous methods supported by citations.

claim: Antibody staining increases the risk of cell loss during the labeling procedure and consequently limits α-cell yield.
source: Both methods enable isolation of live human α-cells with high purity, but require antibody staining, which increases the risk of cell loss during the labeling procedure and consequently limits α-cell yield.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of antibody-based methods.

claim: Antibody-labeling approaches can recover 200,000 α-cells from 10,000 human islet equivalents.
source: It has been reported that antibody-labeling approaches can recover 200,000 α-cells from 10,000 human islet equivalents (IEQ) (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The DA-ZP1 approach can recover ~2×-fold higher live α-cells with ~95% purity compared to antibody-labeling approaches.
source: Here, we provide an antibody-free approach to obtain primary human α-cells using a fluorescein-tagged sensor which can recover ~2×-fold higher live α-cells with ~95% purity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The short incubation (10 min) for labeling with DA-ZP1 followed by sorting reduces effort and limits stress on the cells.
source: Other advantages of the zinc-based labeling approach include: (1) the short incubation (10 min) for labeling with DA-ZP1 followed by sorting which reduces effort and limits stress on the cells; (2) zinc-based probes are cost-effective compared to antibodies and small quantities (80 nM) can be used for multiple experiments which allows scaling up of cell sorting processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the method based on experimental design.

claim: Zinc-based probes are cost-effective compared to antibodies and small quantities (80 nM) can be used for multiple experiments which allows scaling up of cell sorting processes.
source: Other advantages of the zinc-based labeling approach include: (1) the short incubation (10 min) for labeling with DA-ZP1 followed by sorting which reduces effort and limits stress on the cells; (2) zinc-based probes are cost-effective compared to antibodies and small quantities (80 nM) can be used for multiple experiments which allows scaling up of cell sorting processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the method.

claim: Zinc-based probes can bind to intracellular Zn(II) which are important for cell functions including secretion of insulin.
source: In regard to potential disadvantages is the ability of zinc-based probes to bind to intracellular Zn(II) which are important for cell functions including secretion of insulin.
evidence: This is a statement about potential disadvantages based on knowledge of zinc probe properties.

claim: DA-ZP1 does not affect insulin secretion, proliferation, or apoptosis in a human β-cell line (EndoC-βH1) even at high concentrations (10 μM).
source: However, we have shown that DA-ZP1 does not affect insulin secretion, proliferation, or apoptosis in a human β-cell line (EndoC-βH1) even at high concentrations (10 μM) (Kahraman et al., 2021) and therefore this issue may not be a significant concern.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The levels of intracellular DA-ZP1 decrease gradually 24 hr after entering cells by passive diffusion and can last more than a week to disappear completely.
source: Furthermore, since the levels of intracellular DA-ZP1 decrease gradually 24 hr after entering cells by passive diffusion and can last more than a week to disappear completely, further studies are warranted to determine additional effects of DA-ZP1.
evidence: This is a statement about DA-ZP1 properties based on previous observations.

claim: Liu et al. examined the function of re-aggregated α-pseudoislets after sorting individual islet cells by monoclonal surface antibodies.
source: The function of re-aggregated α-pseudoislets was examined previously by Liu et al. after sorting individual islet cells by monoclonal surface antibodies (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In Liu et al.'s study, α-pseudoislets secreted glucagon at low concentrations of glucose but failed to respond to changes in glucose concentrations.
source: In their study, α-pseudoislets secreted glucagon at low concentrations of glucose but failed to respond to changes in glucose concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Liu et al. argued that the glucose-sensing machinery was deregulated in α-pseudoislets in the absence of paracrine effects of neighboring β-cells.
source: They argued that the glucose-sensing machinery was deregulated in the absence of paracrine effects of neighboring β-cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The current study's data demonstrated preserved glucose-sensing machinery and secretory actions of α-pseudoislets despite the absence of β-cells.
source: Conversely, our data demonstrated preserved glucose-sensing machinery and secretory actions of α-pseudoislets despite the absence of β-cells (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by glucagon secretion data shown in Figure 3.

claim: α-cells can regulate glucagon secretion by using cell intrinsic signaling in response to glucose in the absence of paracrine factors and juxtracrine-signaling factors.
source: While our data suggest that α-cells can regulate glucagon secretion by using cell intrinsic signaling in response to glucose in the absence of paracrine factors, such as insulin and somatostatin (Elliott et al., 2015) and juxtracrine-signaling factors, such as EphA4/7 on α-cells and ephrins on β-cells (Reissaus and Piston, 2017), it cannot exclude their contribution to secretory function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on glucagon secretion data and supported by citations.

claim: The current study's data cannot exclude the contribution of paracrine and juxtracrine factors to α-cell secretory function in vivo.
source: While our data suggest that α-cells can regulate glucagon secretion by using cell intrinsic signaling in response to glucose in the absence of paracrine factors, such as insulin and somatostatin (Elliott et al., 2015) and juxtracrine-signaling factors, such as EphA4/7 on α-cells and ephrins on β-cells (Reissaus and Piston, 2017), it cannot exclude their contribution to secretory function in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: RNA-seq data supported maintenance of α-cell identity in α-pseudoislets.
source: Our RNA-seq data supported maintenance of α-cell identity in α-pseudoislets (Figure 4a and b), and demonstrated culture time-dependent adaptive alterations in pathways involved in secretory capacity or glucagon signaling (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RNA-seq data demonstrated culture time-dependent adaptive alterations in pathways involved in secretory capacity or glucagon signaling in α-pseudoislets.
source: Our RNA-seq data supported maintenance of α-cell identity in α-pseudoislets (Figure 4a and b), and demonstrated culture time-dependent adaptive alterations in pathways involved in secretory capacity or glucagon signaling (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The discrepancy between the current study and Liu et al.'s study could be explained by the use of different methods and time points in performing functional assays.
source: Thus, the discrepancy between the two studies could be explained by the use of different methods and time points in performing functional assays.
evidence: This is an inference about the reasons for different results.

claim: Human islets are micro-organs composed of multiple endocrine cell types and feature heterotypic cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions.
source: Human islets are micro-organs composed of multiple endocrine cell types and feature heterotypic cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about islet structure.

claim: Paracrine communication between islet cells are important for their function and proliferation.
source: Earlier studies demonstrated that paracrine communication between islet cells are important for their function and proliferation (Gromada et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Vascular endothelial cells, neuronal projections, and ECM network within the islets contribute regulatory signals to islet cells.
source: Additionally, vascular endothelial cells, neuronal projections, and ECM network within the islets also contribute regulatory signals to islet cells (Aamodt and Powers, 2017; Lammert and Thorn, 2020; Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The islet microenvironment is necessarily disrupted when islets are dissociated into single cells as in unsorted pseudoislets and likely absent in α-pseudoislets.
source: This islet microenvironment is necessarily disrupted when islets are dissociated into single cells as in unsorted pseudoislets and likely absent in α-pseudoislets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Over the 10 days in culture, little change was observed in the transcriptome of native islets compared with unsorted pseudoislets.
source: For example, over the 10 days in culture, we observed little change in the transcriptome of native islets compared with unsorted pseudoislets (Figure 4b, Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 4b and 5a.

claim: The isolation procedure disrupts innervation and vasculature, but isolated islets preserve cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions.
source: Although the isolation procedure disrupts innervation and vasculature, the isolated islets preserve cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of islet isolation.

claim: Almost no changes in the transcriptome of native islets in culture over the period of 10 days highlight the importance of intact islet structure on transcriptome stability.
source: Almost no changes in the transcriptome of native islets in culture over the period of 10 days highlight the importance of intact islet structure on transcriptome stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes involved in ECM organization and cell surface interactions were downregulated in unsorted pseudoislets compared with native islets.
source: Another example of the significance of the islet cell microenvironment is that genes involved in ECM organization and cell surface interactions were downregulated in unsorted pseudoislets compared with native islets (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Previous report showed less abundant ECM components in re-aggregated pseudoislets than in intact islets.
source: These observations are consistent with a previous report showing less abundant ECM components in re-aggregated pseudoislets than in intact islets (Lorza-Gil et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression levels of α- or β-enriched genes were recovered after typical islet architecture was regained in unsorted pseudoislets.
source: A notable finding revealed by RNA-seq data is that expression levels of α- or β-enriched genes were recovered after typical islet architecture was regained in unsorted pseudoislets (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Intact cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions are important to sustain cell identity in vitro.
source: These data support the fact that intact cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions are important to sustain cell identity in vitro (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The expression levels of α-cell enriched genes did not return toward normal in α-pseudoislets despite their ability to self-assemble and form tight clusters.
source: The expression levels of α-cell enriched genes did not return toward normal in α-pseudoislets despite their ability to self-assemble and form tight clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) which might argue that heterotypic cell-to-cell interactions are more important than homotypic interactions in maintaining α-cell identity.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and morphology data.

claim: Heterotypic cell-to-cell interactions are more important than homotypic interactions in maintaining α-cell identity.
source: The expression levels of α-cell enriched genes did not return toward normal in α-pseudoislets despite their ability to self-assemble and form tight clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) which might argue that heterotypic cell-to-cell interactions are more important than homotypic interactions in maintaining α-cell identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq and morphology data.

claim: Previous studies reporting an upregulation of β-cell signature genes in α-cells after monotypic α-cell aggregation or extreme β-cell loss support the relevance of heterotypic cell-to-cell interactions in maintenance of α-cell identity.
source: Indeed, previous studies reporting an upregulation of β-cell signature genes in α-cells after monotypic α-cell aggregation (Furuyama et al., 2019) or extreme β-cell loss (Thorel et al., 2010) support the relevance of heterotypic cell-to-cell interactions in maintenance of α-cell identity.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The tighter cluster formation of α-pseudoislets could be due to preferential expression of adhesion proteins such as N-CAM.
source: The tighter cluster formation of α-pseudoislets was an interesting observation which could be due to preferential expression of adhesion proteins such as N-CAM (neural-cell adhesion molecule) (Cirulli et al., 1994).
evidence: This is speculation based on observation and supported by citation.

claim: RNA-seq data revealed important transcriptional effects secondary to dissociation of human islets.
source: Overall, our RNA-seq data revealed important transcriptional effects secondary to dissociation of human islets and provide a useful resource for future studies on re-aggregated islet cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on RNA-seq data.

claim: The fluorescein-based sensor can be used to isolate live human α-cells for functional studies, transcriptomic analyses, or studies assessing cellular toxicity or proliferation.
source: In conclusion, we report the use of a fluorescein-based sensor, to demonstrate isolation of live pancreatic α-cells with high purity and in vitro cultivation of α-pseudoislets without significantly affecting their identity and function over time. This unique tool can be used to isolate live human α-cells for functional studies, transcriptomic analyses, or studies assessing cellular toxicity or proliferation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the utility of the method.
